headline: Microsoft-backed AI data center faces backlash over 62 unpermitted gas turbines and 1.5M-gallon LNG tank
summary: The $19.4 billion DataOne facility, backed by Microsoft, is accused of operating 62 unpermitted gas turbines, an illegal 1.5M-gallon LNG tank, and causing noise pollution near schools.
details: The DataOne data center in Vineland, New Jersey, has faced numerous complaints from the community since construction began in 2025. Allegations include operating 62 unpermitted gas turbines, an unpermitted 1.5-million-gallon liquefied natural gas storage tank, and causing unacceptable noise levels.

Construction reportedly started before Nebius, which contracted with Microsoft for computing power, signed its multi-year agreement in October 2025. Residents only became aware of the project's nature after a $19.4 billion deal for 100,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs was made public.

References to the data center in government documents prompted questions from Vineland residents, leading to a town hall meeting in January 2026. DataOne CEO Charles-Antoine Beyney admitted the meeting should have been initiated months earlier.

Weeks before the town hall, residents within a half-mile radius reported a low hum, similar to a generator, at night. An investigation revealed 62 gas turbines on site, with at least 45 running at any given time, mirroring a situation with xAI in Memphis.

Concerns also extend to the site's stormwater management system, which a third-party engineering review found non-compliant with state regulations. Unfixed issues could lead to on-site and off-site flooding across the massive 55-acre site.

Experts also noted that the data center underestimated annual groundwater recharge by at least 20 million gallons per year. This could result in lower aquifer levels and reduced water availability or quality for local residents.

Stand.earth Senior Campaigner Nathan Taft stated that the incident "should shatter the illusion that Microsoft is a 'good neighbor'." He compared Microsoft's approach to Elon Musk's xAI playbook of "doing the damage first and asking for permission later."

Although Microsoft does not directly own or operate the Vineland data center, campaigners argue the tech giant should address the complaints. They contend that as the contracting party, Microsoft bears responsibility for the actions of its providers.

DataOne's actions contradict Microsoft's "community-friendly" commitments made in January 2026. While air and noise pollution aren't explicitly mentioned in these commitments, they significantly impact local quality of life and demonstrate a disregard for Vineland's rules.

headline_marked: [[Google Pixel 11]] boasts EU Class B repairability grade
headline: Google Pixel 11 boasts EU Class B repairability grade
summary: Google's latest flagship is designed for disassembly and longevity, with critical spare parts available for seven years post-market.
details: While Google's Made by Google keynote focused heavily on Gemini and the Tensor G6, the Pixel 11's most significant feature might be its repairability. Every Pixel 11 model has earned an official EU repairability grade of Class B, indicating a strong design for disassembly and repair.

This focus on repairability is largely driven by new EU ecodesign rules that took effect in June 2025. These regulations mandate that smartphones be designed for easier disassembly and require manufacturers to provide critical spare parts for seven years after a device is no longer sold.

Beyond ease of repair, the EU rules also target battery longevity. New smartphone batteries must retain at least 80% of their original capacity after 800 full charge cycles, effectively doubling the industry standard and ensuring better battery performance over the device's lifespan.

The Pixel 11's commitment to repairability extends to parts availability. Through a partnership with iFixit, owners can access genuine spare parts and official repair manuals, making DIY repairs more accessible and cost-effective.

While specific pricing for Pixel 11 parts is yet to be finalized, historical data suggests battery kits for recent Pixels range from $40 to $60, and OEM display kits cost between $120 and $260. These costs are manageable when spread over the phone's extended usable life.

In a US PIRG Education Fund scorecard that evaluates repairability, Google received a C-, placing it ahead of Samsung and Apple, though behind Motorola. This score reflects both the EU repair scores and the company's broader Right to Repair policies.

Ultimately, the Pixel 11's dedication to repairability means users can realistically expect to use their device for the full seven years of OS updates. This focus on longevity and user-serviceability is a crucial, often overlooked, aspect of modern smartphone design.
